Steadily means: in a way that is even, smooth, and continuous — without sudden changes, interruptions, or shakiness.

It is the adverb form of the adjective "steady." When something happens steadily, it moves forward with a kind of quiet regularity. No sudden jumps. No random stops. No trembling. Think of it like a river that flows forward calmly, without waterfalls or sudden bends — just smooth, unbroken movement.

1. Gradually, but without stopping

This is the most common meaning. When something changes or progresses "steadily," it keeps moving forward in a consistent, uninterrupted way. It may be slow or fast — but the key is that it doesn't pause, skip around, or suddenly reverse.

  • "The river rose steadily after the rains." → The water level kept going up, bit by bit, without sudden jumps or breaks.
  • "She improved steadily throughout the year." → Her improvement was continuous and reliable — not a big leap one week and nothing for the next two months.
  • "Prices have climbed steadily for a decade." → Up, up, up — consistently, without reversing or pausing.
  • "The patient's condition worsened steadily." → A little worse each day, in a predictable, unbroken pattern.

This sense often carries a sense of dependability. Because the pattern is consistent, you can almost predict what comes next.

2. Without physical shaking or wobbling

When a person holds or does something "steadily," their hands or body are firm and controlled — not trembling, not jerking.

  • "The surgeon's hands moved steadily through the operation." → No shaking at all — total physical control.
  • "He held the camera steadily to avoid a blurry photo." → Completely still, no wobbling.
  • "She carried the full glass of water steadily across the room." → Without spilling, without her hands trembling.
  • "He aimed steadily at the target." → Firm grip, still hand, controlled breathing.

This meaning is entirely about physical stability and control over one's body.

3. In a calm, composed, emotionally controlled way

When someone speaks, looks at someone, or behaves "steadily," they are emotionally in control. They are not panicking, not shaking with fear, not flustered. There is quiet inner strength in this use of the word.

  • "She looked at him steadily, refusing to look away." → Her gaze was calm and unbroken — not darting nervously around.
  • "He answered the questions steadily, even though he was nervous inside." → His voice was even; he showed no sign of falling apart.
  • "Despite the terrible news, she breathed steadily and kept her composure." → No crying, no shouting — just calm, controlled behavior.

This sense carries a connotation of maturity, discipline, and quiet confidence.

Knowing what a word is not sharpens your understanding enormously.

It is not about speed. Steadily says nothing about how fast or slow something is. It only talks about consistency and smoothness. Something can happen steadily at a fast pace or at a slow pace — the word doesn't care which.

"He ran steadily" doesn't tell you he was fast or slow. It tells you his pace was even and consistent throughout.

It is not "sometimes" or "occasionally." If something happens steadily, it doesn't take breaks. "She practiced steadily for months" is very different from "She practiced sometimes for months." The first tells you she practiced regularly, without big gaps.

The opposites of steadily are words like erratically (randomly, unpredictably), jerkily (with sudden movements), fitfully (in bursts with stops in between), and shakily (with trembling). These opposites help you feel the full meaning of steadily by contrast.
How "Steadily" Changes the Feel of a Sentence

Compare these two sentences:

"He slowly got better."
"He steadily got better."

The first just tells you his recovery was slow. The second tells you something richer: his recovery was consistent and uninterrupted — you could see real, reliable progress every day. It almost implies that you could trust the recovery to continue.

This is why "steadily" often carries a quietly positive or reassuring feeling in many contexts. A person who does something steadily comes across as disciplined, reliable, and in control.
Quick Summary of When to Use It

Use steadily when you want to express that:

  • Something is growing, falling, rising, or changing — but in a smooth, consistent, unbroken way (not in sudden leaps).
  • Someone is holding or doing something physically — with a firm, controlled, non-shaking body.
  • Someone is speaking, looking, or behaving — with emotional calm and composure, without cracking under pressure.

The thread running through all three meanings is the same idea: evenness, control, and continuity. That is the soul of this word.
